\chapter{Las --- The Plural Article That Behaves}
\label{ch:articles-las}
\hlchaptermodality{69}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say las casas and las comidas, putting the plural -s on both the article and the noun.}

Complete ES-C44-las: produce las casas and las comidas and say how many new rules the chapter added.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[las casas]{las casas — \textquotedblleft{}the houses\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C44-las}



\begin{quote}
You learned this in your first chapter: a noun ending in a vowel adds \textbf{-s}. So what is \textquotedblleft{}houses\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{Casas}.) Now — what is \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the} houses\textquotedblright{}?
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the article does what the noun does}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{las} — \emph{the}, for more than one feminine thing.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{la casa} $\to$ \emph{\textbf{las} casa\textbf{s}} — the houses. \emph{la comida} $\to$ \emph{\textbf{las} comida\textbf{s}} — the meals.
\end{quote}

The \emph{-s} lands on \textbf{both} words. That is not two rules; it is one rule applied where it belongs. You have already seen Spanish do this — \emph{buenas noches} is \emph{buena} copying \emph{noche}'s number — and it is the same instinct throughout the language: \textbf{the words around a noun agree with it}, so when the noun goes plural, they follow.

So \emph{las} is not a word to memorise. It is \emph{la} obeying the rule you already hold.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}la casa\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}las casas\textquotedblright{} — hear the \emph{-s} twice
  \item \textquotedblleft{}las comidas\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\textquotedblleft{}The houses\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Las casas}}.) Where did the \emph{-s} go? (\textbf{Both} words.) Next: the masculine one, which does not do the obvious thing — and the reason will be familiar.
\end{tcolorbox}
